 Students bridge political division on Election Day, gather for community discussion
 Members of campus political organizations met to find common ground. 
 Nolan Leonard , News reporter 
 • 
 November 16, 2026 
 Categories: 
 News 
 Politics 
 Photo by Madi On Election Day, several students cast their ballots at the Alumni Memorial Union. 
 On Election Day, students at Marquette University sat and searched for common ground in a political climate often characterized by division and animosity. While voters across the country headed to the polls, students took part in a different kind of civic engagement: listening. 
 Members of Marquette College Democrats, Marquette College Republicans and Marquette’s chapter of Young Democratic Socialists of America gathered Nov. 3 for Political Dialogue Night. The event was an opportunity for participants to step beyond party affiliations and engage in conversations about some of the country’s most pressing issues. 
 Unlike ballot boxes, the event didn’t affect policy or domestic affairs. But it reminded students of the power of working together as they moved across the room to talk about the surrounding world. Topics of discussion included the economy, immigration, the midterm elections, AI and data centers and the war in Iran. 
 “I think we found a lot of common ground between the Republicans, the Democrats and the Democratic Socialists,” Cameron Sheehan, a first-year student in the College of Arts & Sciences and member of College Republicans, said. “[With] a lot of issues, we’re a lot closer than we thought we were.” 
 Josh Baker, a senior in the College of Arts & Sciences and treasurer for YDSA, said he realized everyone in the room was more similar than he thought. 
 “I got to shake hands with a Republican and agree about an important issue,” he said. 
 Students with different beliefs found common ground in several discussions, including a conversation about artificial intelligence. Sheehan and Baker initially approached the issue from different sides of the aisle, but as the conversation progressed, they pivoted to listening for perspective rather than listening to respond. 
 As a result, they found commonalities in their opinions on how AI affects education and agreed that AI should be banned in schools. 
 “I am anti-data center and am incredibly fearful of AI,” Sheehan said. “I feel that the cat’s already out of the bag.”
 Other students talked about how fast the technology has evolved and mentioned how they feel it has inhibited the educational experience by limiting the use of textbooks and physical interaction between students and teachers.
 Some attendees, like Ambia Abdikadir, a sophomore in the College of Arts & Sciences, were not members of any of the clubs, but still participated in discussions. 
 “I thought there was a lot of intersectionality between [Republicans and Democrats],” she said. “People were very on the same page about a lot of [topics].” 
 For Sheehan, the conversations represented something larger than talking about policy and finding common ground.   He said many of the challenges facing the country that make it more difficult for Americans to achieve the “American Dream” could be addressed by better communication.  
 Sheehan’s perspective reflected a takeaway shared by several attendants: political disagreement doesn’t have to prohibit people from working towards shared goals.  
 Students that attended Political Dialogue Night didn’t surrender their stances or change their views, but instead found the opportunity to go deeper on issues and recognize the humanity behind them. As they did, they were reminded that people can disagree on a plan of action, but still find commonality in their goals for the country. 
 This article was written by Nolan Leonard. He can be reached at [email protected] .

 About the Contributor 
 Nolan Leonard , News reporter 
 Nolan Leonard is a first-year student studying journalism and political science. He is a news reporter at the Marquette Tribune who joined because he loves to be in the room where things happen and wants to be a storyteller informing our world of the news of the day with a little humor and lots of love. 
Outside of the Wire, Nolan is a Chick Evans Scholar, Campus Minister, and Eucharistic Minister who is involved with Knights of Columbus, Midnight Run, Volunteer Corps, Center for Peacemaking, Best Buddies and the Marquette Mentor program. In his free time, he enjoys listening to music, playing guitar, playing and watching sports, inspiring a world of peace and belonging and being surrounded by quality people.
